title: AWS CWI Training in Norfolk, VA: 6-Day Exam Prep
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Hampton Roads ship repair, shipyard and port welders: corporate, online or one-to-one formats, Parts A, B and C covered.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Norfolk, Virginia: Six Days for Hampton Roads Ship Repair, Shipyard and Port Welding Inspectors
html:
Norfolk's waterfront has been repairing ships for well over a century, and on most days the Elizabeth River is lined with Navy hulls sitting in dry dock or tied up at repair piers. Around that work sits a wider Hampton Roads economy of shipbuilding, container terminals, offshore wind logistics, highway steel and power plants, and every part of it needs people who can judge a weld against a written requirement. Atlantis NDT runs a six-day (6-day) exam-preparation course for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) examination, covering Part A Fundamentals, Part B Practical and Part C Code Application. It comes in three formats: corporate delivery at an employer's facility, online study with an instructor answering questions, and one-to-one sessions for a single candidate. AWS administers the examination and issues the certification; Atlantis prepares candidates and certifies no one. There is no Atlantis classroom in Norfolk. The two Atlantis offices are in Houston, Texas and Hyderabad, India, so Hampton Roads candidates take the course online, in one-to-one sessions or at their employer's site. To scope it, send a Norfolk CWI exam prep enquiry.

How the six days work for a Hampton Roads candidate

The outline tracks the three parts of the exam. Days one and two cover Fundamentals: welding processes and AWS terminology, joint design, welding and weld symbols, metallurgy, destructive and nondestructive testing, discontinuities, fabrication math, safety and the duties of an inspector. Day three rehearses the practical with gauges, measurements and procedure records. Day four is spent inside the code book you have chosen for Part C. Day five is timed practice papers, and day six goes back over weak areas and exam-day logistics. Each block is laid out on the AWS CWI exam prep course page. The same outline sits under all three formats.

Corporate: a yard, contractor or shop preparing a group

A ship repair contractor, subcontractor or fabricator with several people heading for the exam can have all six days delivered at its own facility. The practical day then uses the company's own fillet gauges, bridge cam gauges and real welds, and the code day is pitched at the book most of the group intends to choose.

Online: an individual studying around the waterfront schedule

Individual candidates study online through a study plan built on the six-day outline, with course materials, original practice questions and timed practice papers. An instructor answers questions as you work through them. Nothing runs at a scheduled class time, so the plan bends around twelve-hour shifts, weekend work during a dry-docking and the stretches when an availability is running hot.

One-to-one: one candidate, the instructor's full attention

Six days of one-to-one sessions with the instructor suit someone who learns best by talking problems through, or who needs to close a specific gap such as code navigation or welding symbols. Sessions run online or in person at a location agreed when you book.

The Hampton Roads welding economy, yard by yard

Norfolk is the hub of a region where welding is a core trade rather than a sideline. Most of the work traces back to the Navy, but a growing share does not.

Private ship repair on the Elizabeth River

Several of the country's larger private ship repair yards work within sight of downtown Norfolk. BAE Systems Maritime Solutions Norfolk, on West Berkley Avenue, covers 109 acres and lists the 52,500-ton Titan drydock and the 14,000-ton Old Dominion drydock among its facilities, with the U.S. Navy as its main customer; its apprentice program dates from 1936. General Dynamics NASSCO-Norfolk was formed in 2015 from two older Hampton Roads yards, Metro Machine and Earl Industries. It runs the Ligon Street yard in Norfolk, with a 40,000-long-ton drydock, and the Harper Avenue yard in Portsmouth, and it lists structural and pipe fabrication, welding and NDE among its trades. Colonna's Shipyard, founded in 1875 in the Berkley section on the Eastern Branch of the Elizabeth River, operates three floating dry docks and repairs military, commercial and private vessels and barges, with welding and piping handled through an affiliate company.

The work in these yards is repair and modernization: cropping out wasted plate, renewing foundations, rerouting piping, refurbishing tanks and fitting new systems into older hulls. That mix makes fit-up checks, welder qualification tracking, preheat on thicker structure and visual acceptance of completed welds the everyday business of a waterfront welding inspector.

The public yard across the river

Norfolk Naval Shipyard, despite its name, stands in Portsmouth. It overhauls and repairs naval vessels, submarines included, and runs an apprenticeship whose trade theory is delivered with Tidewater Community College. Its trade list has included shipfitters, pipefitters, boilermakers, sheet metal mechanics and shipwrights, all trades in which weld quality comes up every day. Inspectors who come up through a public yard carry deep knowledge of Navy requirements, and many later want a credential that belongs to them rather than to their employer.

New construction at Newport News

On the Peninsula, Newport News Shipbuilding builds the Navy's aircraft carriers and works on its submarine programs, and it trains new shipbuilders through its own apprentice school. Over a career, plenty of Hampton Roads welders and inspectors move between repair work on the south side and new construction on the north side. For NDT courses on that side of the water, see NDT training in Newport News.

Offshore wind out of Portsmouth Marine Terminal

Dominion Energy's Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project, planned at 176 turbines, loads out from the Portsmouth Marine Terminal. Reporting in August 2026 put the project past 80% complete and generating power since March, with the final turbine installation retargeted for the end of 2027. For local welding inspectors it matters less as a single fabrication job than as another steady source of marine construction, port and vessel work in an already crowded harbor.

Port terminals, bridges and plants

The Port of Virginia's container terminals in Norfolk and Portsmouth bring crane rail, dock steel and heavy equipment repair. Highway bridges and interchanges across the region are fabricated to AWS D1.5, commercial and industrial buildings use structural steel welded to AWS D1.1, and power plants, military installations and water and wastewater plants add pipe welding under the ASME codes. An inspector who can move between the waterfront and these jobs has more than one market to work in.

How Navy repair contracts shape the inspector's job in Norfolk

Navy ship repair is contracted and inspected under Navy documents. Private yards that take Navy work hold agreements with the Navy, such as the Master Ship Repair Agreement that NASSCO-Norfolk lists, and the work items on each availability call up NAVSEA standard items and technical publications for welding, fabrication and inspection. Those documents, rather than an AWS code, set the acceptance criteria on a Navy job, and each yard qualifies its own inspectors to them under its written program.

So where does a CWI fit? In three places. It is a personal credential, so it stays with you when you move from one Elizabeth River yard to another, or from a public yard to a private contractor. It opens work outside the Navy portfolio, from commercial vessels and barges to bridges, buildings and plant piping, where specifications commonly name the CWI. And the exam's coverage of processes, metallurgy, discontinuities and measurement is the background a yard's own qualification builds on. What the CWI does not do is stand in for the Navy-specific qualification your employer's program requires, so ask your quality department how the two relate before planning your next step.

There is a practical consequence for the exam too. AWS offers no Navy option for Part C, so a candidate whose experience is in Navy repair answers code questions from an AWS, API or ASME book. The layout of those books takes practice to navigate under time pressure, and that is what day four of the course is for.

Who hires CWIs around Norfolk, and what they look for

  • Private ship repair contractors. Quality departments at the larger yards need inspectors who can read a work item, check welder qualifications against the job and record acceptance in a form the Navy's representative will sign.
  • Ship repair subcontractors. The big yards rely on smaller firms working under their contracts, from pipe and fabrication shops to specialty trades. The Virginia Ship Repair Association keeps a member directory that works as a map of them, and many need one or two qualified welding inspectors rather than a whole department.
  • Steel fabricators and erectors. Building, bridge and industrial fabricators across Hampton Roads look for CWIs to run shop QC against D1.1 or D1.5.
  • Inspection and testing firms. Third-party firms supply welding inspectors and NDT technicians to owners, engineers and contractors throughout the region.
  • Owners and operators. Utilities, terminal operators and industrial plants keep inspectors to oversee contractors and audit fabricators.

Across these employers the common thread is documentation. A Hampton Roads inspector is valued as much for clean, traceable records as for a sharp eye at the joint.

Choosing the Part C code for Hampton Roads work

Part C is an open-book test on a single code book, and AWS lets you pick it. The options are AWS D1.1 for structural steel, API 1104 for pipelines, AWS D1.2 for aluminum, AWS D1.5 for bridges, AWS D15.1 for railcars and locomotives, AWS D17.1 for aerospace fusion welding, an ASME package that pairs Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3, and an ISO option. For Norfolk work the choice usually narrows to these:

Your welding backgroundBook to considerWhy it fits
Hull structure, decks, foundations, inserts and doublers in ship repairAWS D1.1Its structural steel provisions are the closest AWS match to shipfitting, and the same book governs shore-side structural work
Shipboard piping, boilers, power plant and process pipingASME Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3Procedure and welder qualification variables, plus piping examination and acceptance
Aluminum superstructures, workboats and small craftAWS D1.2Structural welding of aluminum, with its own qualification rules
Bridge girders and highway steelAWS D1.5The bridge welding code used on transportation work
Gas transmission and distribution linesAPI 1104Pipeline welding, qualification and acceptance standards

AWS names a specific edition of each book for the exam, often not the latest one, so get hold of that edition before you start tabbing it. Background reading: AWS D1.1, ASME Section IX, AWS D1.5 and API 1104.

The AWS Tidewater Section and where Norfolk welders learn the trade

The AWS Tidewater Section, part of AWS District 4, takes its name from the Tidewater region around Norfolk. Its technical meetings bring equipment makers and speakers to local members: in October 2026 it hosted Miller Electric's laser trailer, with a talk on hand-held laser welding followed by a hands-on demonstration, and in 2025 it marked National Welding Month with a visit from the AWS national president. It also runs social events such as its annual golf tournament. For a CWI candidate, section meetings are a sensible place to meet working inspectors and QC managers, hear which employers are hiring, and find people who can confirm your welding history on the AWS application.

Most CWIs here started as welders or fitters. Tidewater Community College offers a Career Studies Certificate in welding and a longer Certificate in Welding with general and maritime tracks, and it delivers the trade theory for the Norfolk Naval Shipyard apprenticeship. The private yards train their own people as well; the BAE Systems Norfolk apprentice program now runs full time with a route to a college degree. Schooling matters for the CWI because AWS lets recognized trade and technical courses reduce the years of experience you need, and a documented apprenticeship makes the experience you do claim easier to verify. These programs are part of the region's own training pipeline and are independent of Atlantis.

Booking the exam from Norfolk

The CWI examination is governed by AWS QC1, the 2016 edition with its amendment, and it has three parts, each needing a score of at least 72%. Part A, Fundamentals, is 150 questions. Part B combines hands-on activities with tools and specimens that AWS supplies and 46 questions. Part C is open book, roughly 50 to 65 questions on your chosen code. AWS reports all three on one consolidated score report.

Parts A and C are computer-based tests taken at Prometric test centers; once AWS accepts your application, the confirmation letter carries the eligibility code Prometric asks for when you book. Part B works differently. AWS runs the practical itself, at its own seminar and examination locations and on its own dates, so look up the current AWS schedule for the nearest session in Virginia or the wider Mid-Atlantic and apply in good time. If that session means travel, fit it around your yard's schedule rather than the reverse. AWS publishes its examination fees on aws.org; to plan the wider budget, including time off and travel, see the CWI exam cost planner.

Studying around availabilities, dry dock and shift work

Ship repair moves to the rhythm of availabilities. A ship arrives, the yard opens it up, crews work long days through the heaviest steel and pipe jobs, and pressure peaks in the weeks before undocking and sea trials. Between availabilities the pace eases. Candidates who plan well use the quieter stretches for the fundamentals blocks and keep the timed practice papers for the final fortnight before their Prometric dates.

The online format suits that pattern because nothing runs to a timetable: work through a block on a day off, send the instructor a question at the end of a night shift and pick up again the following week. Carry your Part C book to work and look up the clauses that govern the joints in front of you; ten minutes a day inside the book does more for Part C than a weekend of cramming. For Part B, practise with a fillet gauge and a bridge cam gauge on scrap coupons and cut-outs until reading them is automatic. The Practical NDT welding workshop simulator is another way to rehearse inspection steps when you are away from the shop.

Corporate: six days at a Hampton Roads yard or shop

For an employer, corporate delivery puts the whole course inside the facility where the candidates already work. The practical day uses the company's own gauges and real welds, from welder test plates to production cut-outs, so measuring practice matches what those inspectors will accept on the job. Where it fits, the code day works with the company's own procedures and the book most of the group will choose, and it can be split when shipfitters are heading for D1.1 while pipe welders opt for the ASME package.

Timing is the main planning question in ship repair. The usual answer is a gap between availabilities, or a period when the crew concerned is off the critical path. Each candidate still applies to AWS personally, meets the eligibility and vision rules personally and books their own exam; the employer can support that process but cannot file anything on a candidate's behalf.

One-to-one sessions for a single Hampton Roads candidate

In this format one candidate gets six days of sessions with the instructor and nobody else in the room. It fits a QA inspector being prepared for a lead role who needs to tighten up code navigation, a pipefitter whose fundamentals are solid but whose metallurgy is rusty, or a sailor leaving the Navy who wants to turn years of hull maintenance into a civilian credential. Sessions run online, or in person at a location agreed when booking, and the time goes on that candidate's weak areas rather than a group average.

Eligibility and the vision record for Hampton Roads candidates

AWS sets the experience you need by your level of education: five years of welding-related work with a high school diploma, fewer with recognized trade courses or a degree, and more with less schooling. The experience has to be verifiable work on welded products, such as production, repair, construction or inspection, and AWS alone decides what counts. Navy and shipyard experience can count, provided it is documented with dates, ratings or job titles and someone who can confirm it. AWS also requires an eye examination on its Visual Acuity Record: near vision of Jaeger J2 at 12 inches or more, corrected or not, plus a color perception test, performed by a qualified practitioner and recent enough at exam time. Candidates short of the CWI experience sometimes take the AWS Certified Associate Welding Inspector (CAWI) credential first. The full eligibility table is on the CWI exam prep course page, and the CWI requirements guide covers the details.

After the CWI: career paths in Hampton Roads

AWS keeps the CWI valid for nine years, with renewals due at the third and sixth years and recertification at the ninth. Hampton Roads inspectors tend to build in one of three directions.

  • Senior CWI and QA leadership. Inspectors who end up running a yard's or contractor's welding quality program often aim for the AWS Senior CWI; see the Senior CWI pathway. AWS endorsements on additional codes widen the work you can sign for.
  • NDT methods. Ship repair depends on ultrasonic thickness readings, magnetic particle testing of structural welds and penetrant testing of stainless and nonferrous piping. Performing those tests needs method training and certification by the employer under its written practice. Atlantis provides training built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A in VT, MT, PT and UT; see maritime NDT training in Norfolk, NDT training in Norfolk, UT Level 2, MT Level 2 and VT Level 2.
  • Shore-side structural and bridge work. A CWI with D1.1 or D1.5 experience can move into fabrication QC or special inspection on construction projects.

If you are weighing credentials, the CWI, API 577 and ASNT Level II comparison sets them side by side, and the breakdown of CWI results by part shows where candidates tend to struggle. For local NDT services, see ultrasonic testing in Norfolk and magnetic particle testing in Norfolk.

Other East Coast CWI pages and requesting a quote

Candidates elsewhere in the region can read the CWI exam prep pages for Washington, DC, Baltimore, Charlotte and North Charleston.

For a quote, tell us whether the course is for one person or a group and which format you want, outline each candidate's schooling and welding history, name the Part C book each one is aiming for, and, for corporate delivery, give the facility location, the gauges and weld samples available and any availability schedule to work around. Use the Norfolk CWI enquiry form.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis CWI classroom in Norfolk?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Norfolk. Atlantis keeps offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and Hampton Roads candidates take the six-day course in one of three formats: online with an instructor answering questions, as six days of one-to-one sessions (online or in person at an agreed location), or as a corporate course at their employer's facility. See the course outline.

faq.q: Who issues the CWI, AWS or Atlantis?
faq.a: AWS. AWS administers the examination, scores all three parts and issues the certification to candidates who pass. The Atlantis course prepares you for that exam; AWS has not approved, accredited or endorsed it.

faq.q: I am a shipfitter on Navy repair work. Which Part C code should I choose?
faq.a: Most shipfitters choose AWS D1.1, because its structural steel provisions are the nearest AWS match to hull, deck and foundation work, and the same book opens shore-side structural jobs. Pipefitters and boiler workers often prefer the ASME package of Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3. See AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Does a CWI replace the inspector qualification my yard requires for Navy work?
faq.a: No. Navy ship repair is inspected to NAVSEA requirements, and each yard qualifies its inspectors under its own written program. The CWI is a personal credential that travels with you between employers and opens commercial, construction and plant work; ask your quality department how it fits alongside the Navy qualification.

faq.q: Where do Norfolk candidates take the CWI exam?
faq.a: Fundamentals and Code Application are computer-based tests booked through Prometric using the eligibility code in your AWS confirmation letter. The practical is run by AWS at its own seminar and examination locations on its own dates, so check the AWS schedule for the nearest session and plan any travel around your yard's work.

faq.q: Can a ship repair contractor have the six days delivered at its yard?
faq.a: Yes. Corporate delivery brings all six days to your facility and uses your gauges, test plates and production cut-outs. It is usually timed for a gap between availabilities, and the code day can be split between D1.1 and the ASME package. Send an enquiry.

faq.q: What is the difference between one-to-one online and one-to-one in person?
faq.a: Both give a single candidate six days of sessions with the instructor, built around that person's weak areas. Online sessions suit people on rotating shifts; in-person sessions take place at a location agreed when you book.

faq.q: Are the practice questions taken from the AWS exam?
faq.a: No. Every practice question and timed paper is original, written by Atlantis to the topic areas AWS publishes. Atlantis never sees the AWS exam itself, its questions or anyone's answers.

faq.q: Does my Navy service count toward the CWI experience requirement?
faq.a: It can. AWS decides what counts, and it looks for verifiable welding-related work on welded products. List each assignment with dates, rating or job title, the kind of welding work you did and someone who can confirm it. The requirement also depends on your education; see CWI requirements.

faq.q: Can I add NDT methods after the CWI?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis provides training built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A in VT, MT, PT and UT, after which your employer certifies you under its written practice. See maritime NDT training in Norfolk and NDT training in Norfolk.
